To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

historical rainforest contractions and localized extinctions have been the key processes in the formation of the patterns of species richness, regional endemism and distribution patterns in the rainforets of Australia's wet tropical region.

the spatial patterns in the distribution of vertebrates in Australia's wet tropical rainforests are congruent for all classes, the proportion of regionally endemic vertebrates is strongly related to the shape of subregions, and the number of regionaly endemic species in a region is strongly related to subregional shape and area, and that these patterns are congruent with the hypothesis that the current distribution of vertebrates has been strongly influenced by historical contractions of rainforests.

The number of regionally endemics and the proportion of regionally endemic vertebrate species in each subregion of Australia's rainforests are both strongly related (i) to the geographic shape (area and length) of the subregioanl patch of rainforest, and (ii) to the number of species that are shared with other subregions.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the spatial patterns in the distribution of vertebrates in Australian tropical rainforeasts, and how these patterns are related to the history of rainforest contraction and subsequent extinctions.
the processes of regional extinction and speciation that have led to the patterns of endemisms and species richness that we see today in the rainforest biogeographic region.
the historical processes that have influenced current vertebrate distributions in the rainforeasts of the wet tropic biogeographic region.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

historical habitat contractions, coupled with localized extinctions, and the current shape of rainforest patches, are the major processes that have shaped current patterns of species richness, endemism and nested distribution patterns in the rainforets of the wet tropic biogeographic region in Australia.

localized extinctions (i.e. species sifting) have been the most important process in determining the current patterns of endemics and species richness in Australian tropical rainforeasts, with the relative importance of this process varying among subregions.
the rainforests in the wet tropics are not only the oldest rainforests in Australia, but they are also the most diverse and the most endemic.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

historical habitat contractions, coupled with species sifting, have been extremely important in the formation of the patterns of species richness, and especially endemism, in the rainforeasts of the wet tropic region of north–easteern Australia.

the rainforest of the wet tropic bioregion has experienced a history of contraction and fragmentation, and this has led to a pattern of nested distributions of vertebrate species, with the number of species and number of endemics in each subregion being strongly correlated with the geographic shape of each subregion.

the patterns of vertebrate distributions are consistent with historical contractions of the rainforests, coupled with localized extinctions, as being the most important processes in the formation of the current patterns of vertebrate species richness and endemism in this rainforest biogeographic region.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the combination of area and shape are a useful predictor of patterns of species richness, endemism, and nestedness in rainforests, with implications for the management and conservation of rainforest biodiversity.
, for the vertebrate fauna, the wet tropics region of Australia can be viewed as a series of subregions that have been shaped by historical rainforest contractions.
the patterns of species richness, endemism and distributional structure are consistent with a historical hypothesis of rainforest contraction and localized species sifting.
